site.name: Unnati Index
site.description: Rankings and comparisons of Indian states across the economy, jobs, health, education, safety, governance, infrastructure, environment and inclusion, refreshed automatically from official sources.

home.status: Early preview. Data pipelines are being connected; rankings will appear here as official data loads.
home.pillarsIntro: The Unnati Index combines about 40 indicators into eight equally weighted pillars. Every indicator is a rate or per-person value, so large states don't win just by size.

principles.title: Fair comparisons
principles.body: States are ranked within peer groups (large states, North-East and Himalayan states, Union Territories) as well as overall.

principles.title: Progress, not just position
principles.body: Fixed goalposts mean a state's score rises only when its own numbers improve. Every leaderboard also shows who improved most.

principles.title: Honest about freshness
principles.body: Every number shows the period it covers, when we fetched it and when the next official release is expected.

principles.title: Accountable, not partisan
principles.body: Each figure is linked to the office-holders in charge during the period it describes, not just today's. Methodology, code and data are public.

indicators.intro: Every indicator we track, grouped by topic. Indicators in a pillar feed the Unnati Index; the rest are shown for context.

rules.title: Rates, not totals
rules.body: Every ranked indicator is a rate, share or per-person value, so large states don't win just by size.

rules.title: Fixed goalposts
rules.body: Each indicator is scored 0-100 between two fixed goalposts. The best end is a national or SDG target where one exists, otherwise the 97.5th percentile of state values since 2015; the worst end is the 2.5th percentile. Goalposts stay fixed for a methodology version, so a score only rises when the state's own numbers improve. Very skewed per-person values (income, exports, electricity) are scored on a log scale, as UNDP does for income, so going from 10 to 100 counts as much as from 100 to 1,000.

rules.title: One period for everyone
rules.body: Each indicator compares states on a common period when at least 80% of them report it (for example, everyone on NFHS-5 until NFHS-6 covers most states). Otherwise each state's latest value is used, and the period is shown next to every number. Values more than six years old are not used.

rules.title: Pillars and the index
rules.body: A pillar is the average of its indicator scores, computed only when at least 60% of its indicators have data. The Unnati Index is the average of the eight pillars, computed only when at least six have scores. Gaps are never filled in silently.

rules.title: Ranks and bands
rules.body: States are ranked within peer groups (large states; North-East and Himalayan states; Union Territories) and overall. Equal scores at one decimal share a rank. Bands follow NITI Aayog's: Achiever (100), Front Runner (65-99), Performer (50-64), Aspirant (below 50).

rules.title: Progress
rules.body: Earlier editions are recomputed with the same goalposts, using only data for periods that had ended by then, so 'most improved' compares like with like.

changes.body: The Inclusion pillar adds violence against women by their husbands, from the NFHS household survey, which counts violence that is never reported to the police. The Gender Equality and Social Progress indices use it instead of registered crimes against women, which are highest where reporting is easiest; the Safety Index keeps registered crime. All other goalposts are unchanged, so only this moves the scores: Andhra Pradesh moves from 8th to 9th among large states, and Assam falls from 50.0 to 49.3.
First published version: fixed goalposts, eight equal-weight pillars.

sources.title: Data sources
sources.intro: Every dataset, where it comes from and when we last checked it. The pipeline checks each source daily and loads only new or revised figures.

indices.title: Indices
indices.intro: Composite indices built only from the official data on this site, each modelled on a well-known international index. They use the same fixed goalposts as the Unnati Index, so scores rise only when a state's own numbers improve.
indices.otherBody: Consumption inequality (Gini) and multidimensional poverty (MPI) are published officially for every state, so we show them directly rather than rebuilding them.
indices.notBuiltBody: Happiness, democracy, press freedom, freedom and corruption-perception indices rest on surveys of how people feel or on expert ratings of rights, elections and the media. No official state-level data measures these, and stand-ins (such as corruption cases registered, which reflect enforcement rather than corruption) would mislead, so we leave them out.
indices.scaleNote: Score out of 100. Darker means a higher score.

compare.title: Compare states
compare.intro: Put two to four states or UTs side by side on the Unnati Index, its pillars and every indicator. The best value in each row is marked.
compare.choose: Choose at least two states or UTs to compare.
compare.differentPeriods: Not marked: the latest figures are for different periods.

pillar.method: The pillar score is the average of these indicators' scores. Each indicator is scaled from 0 to 100 between fixed goalposts, so a score rises only when the state's own figure improves. A state needs data for at least 60% of the indicators to get a pillar score.

updates.title: Data updates
updates.intro: Every time the pipeline loads new or revised official figures, it is listed here: which source, which periods and which indicators. Revisions keep the earlier figures on record.

cities.title: Cities
cities.intro: Every city with more than 4 lakh people in the 2011 Census, plus each state and UT capital: {n} cities. Air quality updates daily from CPCB's bulletin and annual PM2.5 comes from CPCB's monitoring networks; crime figures cover NCRB's 19 metropolitan cities. Cleanliness, municipal finances and metro rail will follow.
cities.crimeCaveat: NCRB calculates city crime rates on each city's 2011 Census population, so rates are overstated for cities that have grown since. Registered crime also depends on how easily people can report it.
cities.noAqi: No CPCB monitoring station in the daily bulletin
cities.mapNote: Dot size shows population (Census 2011). Darker means worse air. Select a city for its report card.
cities.crimeIntro: NCRB publishes city crime figures only for the 19 cities over 2 million people.
cities.stateMapIntro: {n} cities. Select one for its report card.
cities.noCities: No city in {state} is in the roster yet (cities over 4 lakh people, plus capitals).
cities.pm25Note: India's annual standard is 40 µg/m³; WHO's guideline is 5.
cities.insetNote: Crowded areas are repeated below, enlarged.
cities.superLeagueNote: One of the past top performers, assessed separately and not scored.

data.title: Download the data
data.intro: Every figure on this site as CSV: each indicator for every state, UT and city, with its period, source and notes. Files open in Excel, Google Sheets or any analysis tool.
